dietEvidence.body: Tooth marks on sauropod and conspecific bones show that Majungasaurus fed on both. The marks do not establish whether it killed its prey or scavenged. Cannibalism is documented as feeding on conspecifics, not necessarily predation.

sizeNote: Length and mass are estimates from incomplete material, not measurements of a whole animal.
tagline: An abelisaurid with a short, deep skull and very small forelimbs. Tooth marks on bones show it fed on other Majungasaurus, but whether this was predation or scavenging is unclear.
summary: An abelisaurid with a short, deep skull and very small forelimbs. Tooth marks on bones show it fed on other Majungasaurus, but whether this was predation or scavenging is unclear.

discovery.body: Named by Depéret, 1896. The record is known from Maevarano Formation, Mahajanga Basin. Several skulls and partial skeletons, including evidence of cannibalism.

fossilEvidence.title: Preserved material
fossilEvidence.body: Several skulls and partial skeletons, including evidence of cannibalism.

fossilEvidence.title: Stratigraphic and geographic occurrence
fossilEvidence.body: Maevarano Formation, Mahajanga Basin records the species in the Late Cretaceous. The numeric range used here is ≈70–66 Ma, an occurrence estimate rather than a direct date on every specimen.

fossilEvidence.title: Feeding traces
fossilEvidence.body: Tooth-marked bones from multiple Majungasaurus individuals preserve marks that match the size, spacing and serration spacing of Majungasaurus teeth. They show feeding on conspecifics; they do not distinguish predation from scavenging.

anatomy.title: Preserved anatomy
anatomy.body: The skull is short and deep, with a rugose nasal region and a tall, narrow lower jaw. A virtually complete skull has clarified the craniofacial anatomy and extensive ossification.

anatomy.title: Body plan
anatomy.body: The forelimbs are short and robust, with reduced muscle lever arms compared with more basal theropods. The reduction is documented by osteology and reconstructed myology.

behaviour.body: The tooth marks are direct evidence of feeding behaviour. Social hunting, parental care and other behaviour are unknown.

reconstruction.body: A licensed life reconstruction is assigned to this record and credited in Sources and credits. The species is known from several skulls and partial skeletons, including evidence of cannibalism. The reconstruction is an artist's interpretation of appearance, not a direct observation from the fossil record; preserved integument, where present, is described in the anatomy section, and the soft-tissue outline is otherwise inferred.

confidenceNote: The skull and forelimb anatomy are well described, and tooth marks on conspecific bones provide direct evidence of feeding on Majungasaurus. Whether this was predation or scavenging is not established. Rogers et al. (2003) attributed the marks to Majungasaurus on the basis of tooth size, spacing and serration spacing.
